title: Fra Angelico's cells
hook: each friar's cell at San Marco has its own fresco to pray with

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yves Congar: silenced, obedient, and later called in to help shape a council. Your line was vindicated later. Where did you answer a misunderstanding once, and let the rest wait? Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

A stone staircase in an old friary in Florence. You climb it, turn at the top, and there on the wall in front of you is an angel, wings striped like a bird's, bowing to a young woman on a bench. Mary leans forward, arms crossed over her chest, listening. The colors are soft, the room in the painting is plain, almost empty. Then you walk down the corridor, and every small doorway opens on a bare room with a single window, a bed's worth of floor, and one more painting on the wall. A different one in each. This is San Marco, and the painter was a friar who lived there. Today's word is what he left in their rooms.
screen: `A STAIRCASE IN FLORENCE.` → `AN ANGEL BOWS TO MARY.` → `ONE PAINTING IN EVERY ROOM.`

segments.voice: The painter was a Dominican, Fra Giovanni, remembered as Fra Angelico, the angelic brother. With his workshop he painted frescoes on the walls of the friars' cells, the small rooms where each brother slept, studied and prayed. These were not made for visitors. They were made for one man at a time, to pray with, alone. That changes how you look at them. They are quiet on purpose: few details, plain backgrounds, nothing to distract. And in several of them there's a surprise. Off to the side of the Gospel scene stands a Dominican friar, sometimes Saint Dominic himself, kneeling or reading or simply watching. The friar in his cell looks at the wall and sees a friar inside the story. The painting is saying: this is where you belong, at the edge of the scene, paying attention. At the top of the stairs, the Annunciation sets the tone for the whole house. Luke's Gospel gives Mary's answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." Listening, then yes. That's the Dominican rhythm we've followed all week, in different clothes. Rose and Martin in Lima. An honest look at the Inquisition and forgiveness asked. Lacordaire back in France. Laypeople with a study group. A climber in Turin. A theologian who waited. And here, a painter who gave each brother a window into the Gospel, right next to his real window. Pray, study, share, and sometimes the sharing is a wall.
screen: `A DOMINICAN PAINTER: FRA ANGELICO.` · `MADE FOR ONE FRIAR AT A TIME.` · `A FRIAR STANDS INSIDE THE SCENE.` · `THIS WEEK: DOMINICANS IN MANY CLOTHES.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put an image where you pray, or where you sit still. Look around your space and choose one spot at eye level: a shelf, a corner of a desk, the wall beside your bed. Then choose what could go there: a small icon, a print of a painting, a photo of a place that quiets you, even a postcard. For now, just look at the empty spot and breathe, the way a friar might sit with his wall. If you pray, you can let Mary's answer, be it done to me, rest there. The bell holds the time.
Fra Angelico's cells. The rooms at San Marco in Florence, each with its own quiet fresco, painted by a Dominican friar for his brothers to pray with. Today's word.
Your line: a painting in each cell. Today, put one image in the spot you chose, and look at it once before you sleep. Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Some Catholics keep an icon, a crucifix or a holy picture in the place they pray at home, and San Marco in Florence, now a museum, still shows Fra Angelico's frescoes in the friars' cells.
